name: Smaply
tagline: Web tool for building personas, customer journey maps and stakeholder maps that other people can actually read.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Underneath the CX vocabulary this is a structured diagram editor: stages across the top, lanes down the side, cards in cells, an emotion curve drawn over the whole thing. An agent can absolutely build that in a weekend, and the data model is the easy part. What it will not nail in one sitting is the boring stuff that makes journey maps useful to other people: clean multi-page PDF and slide export, shared links for stakeholders who will never install anything, image handling for personas, and the hundred small layout decisions that keep a 12-stage map legible. If the map lives on your own screen and you present by screen sharing, the DIY version is genuinely fine. If your deliverable is a document that gets sent to a client, budget more than a weekend.
coreLoopDIY: A local lane-and-stage journey map editor with personas, touchpoint cards, an emotion curve, and JSON plus print export.
requirements: a browser you are willing to print to PDF from
whatYouLose: Presentation-grade export: PDF, PowerPoint, PNG at sizes that survive a projector
Share links for stakeholders who will not run a dev server
Prebuilt templates and the shared vocabulary that makes a team's maps look consistent
Persona image libraries, hierarchy between maps, and the general absence of layout bugs
moatNotes: The artifact is a deliverable, so export fidelity and shareability are most of the product value, not the editor.
whyPeopleStillPay: Journey maps are made to be shown to someone with budget authority. Teams pay so that the map arrives as a tidy PDF or a link, looks the same as the last one, and can be edited by the colleague who owns the research without a handoff. A local build gives you the thinking tool and skips the delivery layer, which is exactly the half that consultants are being paid for.
notes: The editor is a weekend; the export pipeline is the part that quietly eats a week.
prompt:
Build a local-first customer journey mapping tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, use exactly this: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, Zustand for state, no backend.
Persistence: everything in localStorage, plus explicit Import JSON and Export JSON buttons. One JSON file is the whole document.

Data model:
- Project: id, name, personas[], maps[]
- Persona: id, name, role, quote, needs[], painPoints[], optional imageDataUrl
- Map: id, name, personaId, stages[], lanes[], cards[], emotionPoints[]
- Stage: id, label, order
- Lane: id, label, type of 'touchpoints' | 'actions' | 'channels' | 'pains' | 'opportunities' | 'custom', order
- Card: id, stageId, laneId, text, optional color
- EmotionPoint: stageId, value from -2 to 2

UI:
- Left sidebar: project tree, personas, maps. Create, rename, delete.
- Main canvas: a CSS grid, stages as columns, lanes as rows, cards inside cells. Add card by clicking an empty cell. Inline edit text. Drag cards between cells using HTML5 drag and drop, no drag library.
- An emotion curve rendered as an inline SVG polyline directly above the grid, aligned to stage columns, points draggable vertically.
- Persona editor: simple form, image via file input converted to a data URL.
- Horizontal scroll for wide maps with sticky lane labels and sticky stage headers.

Export: a print stylesheet so Cmd+P produces a clean landscape map with the emotion curve, plus a PNG export of the canvas using html-to-image.

Out of scope, do not build: auth, sharing links, real-time collaboration, comments, PowerPoint export, template gallery, analytics.

Seed the app with one example project: a 6-stage "buying a bike online" map with 4 lanes and a filled emotion curve, so the tool is not empty on first load.
Write a README with run instructions and the JSON schema. Vitest tests for the store reducers only.
